value: nocturnal (94 of 127 night-time records, 74.02%) and crepuscular (33 of 127, 25.98%) activity
method: citizen-science and personal field records of night-time activity (iNaturalist 1992-2022, Observation.org 2012-2022, authors' observations 2010-2023); records classed by time of observation: crepuscular = 15 min before sunset to 30 min after, nocturnal = more than 30 min after sunset (Methods, after Dyugmedzhiev et al. 2020)
conditions: Free-ranging common grass snakes, mostly Europe (authors' own records mostly Romania). This record: 127 night-time activity records (133 individual snakes: 34 crepuscular and 99 nocturnal, as some records showed more than one active snake), of 9,745 iNaturalist records downloaded to 22 February 2023 plus 22 personal and 12 Observation.org records. The 127 are records selected for crepuscular or nocturnal activity, so the 74.02% and 25.98% split night-time records and are not shares of the species' whole activity. The Abstract opens by calling the species traditionally considered diurnal, with scarce evidence of crepuscular and nocturnal activity; the paper reports that nocturnal activity is geographically widespread. No captive animals.

method: citizen-science camera traps; only independent events kept; hourly activity of squirrels analysed from 1,335 pictures taken at 170 stations (Results 3.2.1)
conditions: Free-ranging urban Eurasian red squirrels, private gardens in Berlin, Germany; camera traps set by volunteers at about 50 cm height with a clear view across the garden, for 4 consecutive weeks in each of five project phases (autumn 2018, spring and autumn 2019, spring and autumn 2020); the first phase was omitted from the analyses; the page does not say whether cameras were baited. This record: 1,335 independent squirrel pictures from 170 stations (Results 3.2.1). The same sentence also classes cats (active throughout the day) and martens (primarily crepuscular and nocturnal); this record takes the squirrel clause. The Results also say squirrels were active between 5am and 5pm. The Results give 'collected via 346 stations' for the pictures of all three taxa, and Methods say 346 of 516 stations did not detect any squirrels, so the paper's station counts are not consistent; 170 stations is the figure given for the squirrel hourly analysis.
